claims.text: TaVCrW is considered as a disordered BCC solid and as a liquid between 2000 K and 2400 K.
The TaVCrW solid exhibits short-range order.
TaVCrW has relevant electronic density-of-states features near the Fermi level.
Using an MTP with FEP instead of an EAM reference with TI will reduce computational cost by more than 80%.
The proposed MTP-FEP calculation will agree with the DFT-TI benchmark to within 0.5 meV/atom.
Short-range order stabilizes the TaVCrW solid by approximately 2-3 meV/atom.
Electronic excitation or DOS-gap effects in the liquid influence the TaVCrW melting calculation.
An MTP can serve as a computationally efficient, sub-meV-accurate surrogate in high-temperature TaVCrW thermodynamic calculations.
The MTP accurately reproduces the ab initio solid and complex-liquid phase-space distributions.
Reproducing the local atomic environments responsible for SRO is necessary for the MTP to capture the stated stabilization energy.
FEP can estimate the relevant free-energy differences from one ensemble or a small number of windows.
Replacing TI with FEP avoids sampling the entire reversible integration path with expensive DFT forces.
The accuracy of FEP is contingent on the reference MTP reproducing SRO and electronic effects.
A supercell containing more than approximately 1000 atoms is needed to resolve a 2-3 meV/atom SRO contribution.
Sampling from 2000 K to 2400 K is sufficient to validate electronic-excitation effects relevant to melting.
Electronic excitations associated with a DOS gap at the Fermi level can shift the melting point by tens of kelvin.
High-temperature magnetic fluctuations are generally neglected but may materially alter the free-energy landscape or melting point.
The usual GGA-PBE underbinding and LDA overbinding rules do not hold for V and Cr at 0 K.
The baseline TOR-TILD treatment uses an EAM reference potential and thermodynamic integration.
Binary Ta-V or Ta-Cr provides a simpler benchmark with a melting point well characterized by DFT-TI.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis describes a 'melting temperature error' using meV/atom, while the falsification rule applies the same 0.5 meV/atom threshold interchangeably to melting-temperature differences and free-energy differences. Temperature and energy-per-atom errors are distinct quantities unless an explicit thermodynamic conversion is supplied.
